title: Role of Interfacial Coherency on Creep Behavior of FCC/BCC High-Entropy Alloy Multilayers.

recollection.starting_material: Alternating nanoscale layers of an FCC high‐entropy alloy (e.g. equimolar CoCrFeMnNi) and a BCC high‐entropy alloy (e.g. equimolar AlCoCrFeNi)
recollection.intervention: Magnetron‐sputter deposition to produce multilayers with controlled layer thickness and interface chemistry, followed by selective annealing treatments to tune interface coherency; high‐temperature creep testing at 600–800 °C under 50–200 MPa
recollection.structure: Periodic FCC/BCC multilayer with individual layer thicknesses of 50–200 nm and either coherent (lattice‐matched) or semi‐coherent/incoherent interfaces
recollection.mechanism: Coherent interfaces impose a strong barrier to dislocation climb and glide, forcing dislocations to bow or transmit less easily; incoherent interfaces allow more interface sliding and diffusional creep pathways
recollection.results: Samples with coherent FCC/BCC interfaces exhibited a ~5× lower steady‐state creep rate compared with incoherent samples; stress exponent increased from ~3.5 to ~5.0 and activation energy rose by ~30 kJ/mol (to ~280 kJ/mol) in the coherent‐interface condition (best‐guess values).

score.note: The recollection correctly mentions sputtered FCC/BCC multilayers with varied layer thickness/coherency, but invents annealing and conventional high-temperature creep instead of 8–80 nm modulation periods followed by nanoindentation creep. The structural description is generic and gives incorrect thicknesses. The mechanism is reversed: semicoherent M16 interfaces, not coherent interfaces, provided the strongest obstruction and best creep resistance. All reported numerical trends and values are inconsistent with the paper.
